storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Moonshot AI resets Kimi K3.1 Pro quotas after user complaints

prior_narrative.tldr: On Oct 16, coverage framed Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 as a name without a released model, and one report said a new Chinese export-license requirement for large AI models could affect it. A week later, reports said it was being readied for release after Arena testing.
prior_narrative.whats_new: On Oct 23, TestingCatalog reported Kimi K3.1 is being prepared for release after Arena testing, and R&D World published a comparison of Kimi K3.1 Pro against Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: A pre-release open-weight candidate with a possible export-licensing hurdle is a planning risk: availability, hosting terms and timing are unconfirmed.

status.detail: Kimi K3.1 appears to be nearing release after Arena testing, but the headlines here do not confirm a launch date or availability.

beats.headline: Kimi K3.1 discussed before any model ships; export-license rule flagged
beats.summary: Oct 16 items: a name-only comparison piece and a report on a Chinese export-license requirement for new large AI models.

beats.headline: Release prep after Arena testing, plus head-to-head comparison
beats.summary: Oct 23 items: release-readiness report and a comparison with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra.

open_questions: Does Moonshot publish Kimi K3.1 weights or an API with a confirmed release date?
Does the reported Chinese export-license requirement delay or restrict the K3.1 release?
Do independent evals confirm the Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra comparison claims?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Do not wire Kimi K3.1 into production routing yet; queue an eval on your own tasks for when weights or an API appear, and check the license and hosting terms then.

storylines.label: Their Own
storylines.latest_title: Why founders keep failing to vibecode their own LLM inference engine

prior_narrative.tldr: "Their Own" groups three items that share a phrase, not one developing event. They run from a Oct 14 paper on distilling web agents from black-box teachers to an Oct 21 study of models rewriting their own harness.
prior_narrative.whats_new: A Startup Fortune piece on Oct 24 argues founders keep failing when they try to vibecode their own LLM inference engine; only the headline was available, so its evidence is unverified.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: All three touch the build-versus-depend question for agent stacks: distill a cheaper agent, let the model tune its own scaffold, or write your own serving layer. None yet gives production evidence.

status.detail: Three unrelated items sharing a phrase; no single event is unfolding.

beats.headline: Web agents trained from a black-box teacher in the teacher's own style
beats.summary: Paper targets the inference cost of closed-model web agents by supervising smaller open models.

beats.headline: Controlled ARC-AGI-3 study asks whether LLMs can improve their own harness
beats.summary: Research on models modifying the symbolic scaffold around them instead of humans redesigning it per task.

beats.headline: Commentary: founders keep failing to vibecode their own inference engine
beats.summary: News-search item; only the headline and outlet were available.

open_questions: Do the harness-improvement results on ARC-AGI-3 hold on production agent tasks outside that benchmark?
Does the black-box distillation approach match its closed-model teacher on web-agent success rate at lower inference cost?
Does the Startup Fortune piece name concrete failure modes of self-built inference engines, such as throughput, memory or batching?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Do not replace a maintained inference server (vLLM, SGLang or a hosted API) with a self-written engine on the strength of this piece; keep the existing stack until a source shows benchmarked results.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

prior_narrative.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of RL items, not one developing story. Since Oct 12 it has collected a Qwen long-horizon agent report, an O-RAN benchmark, and four Oct 20-22 arXiv papers on training tool-using and search agents.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Oct 23: AWS publishes a hands-on guide to multi-turn RL on Amazon SageMaker AI, training on whole-task outcomes with a Wordle example.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: The SageMaker guide is the first managed-platform recipe in the thread, so teams on AWS can try outcome-based multi-turn RL without building the training harness. The arXiv papers cover rollout cost, stateful environments, search-state awareness and per-decision credit assignment; QwenGyre (a secondary-source report) and X-RIC remain research or telecom-specific.

status.detail: A loose set of agentic-RL items; the newest moves from papers to a managed-platform guide.

beats.headline: Alibaba Qwen introduces QwenGyre for elastic RL on extra-long-horizon agents
beats.summary: Reported via MarkTechPost; targets agent tasks that run far longer than standard RL rollouts.

beats.headline: X-RIC benchmarks agentic RAN controllers for reinforcement learning
beats.summary: Targets O-RAN controllers rather than LLM post-training.

beats.headline: Agentic RL papers: rollout budgets, stateful environments, search-state awareness, credit assignment
beats.summary: Four arXiv papers on cutting rollout cost, extending RL beyond tool-centric settings, teaching search agents to assess their own state, and crediting individual decisions within an episode.

beats.headline: AWS walks through multi-turn RL on SageMaker AI
beats.summary: A hands-on pipeline that trains on the outcome of a whole multi-step task, demonstrated on Wordle.

open_questions: Does calibrated rollout budgeting cut MCP-agent training cost on benchmarks beyond the paper's own?
Does BIRD-RL's gain on small language models hold on larger models?
Does Qwen publish QwenGyre weights, code, or benchmarks that show the elastic RL gain on long-horizon agent tasks?
Does the SageMaker MTRL recipe carry from Wordle to tool-using agent tasks, and at what training cost?
Does twin-world credit assignment improve agent training on benchmarks beyond the paper's own?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you train tool-using models, read the rollout-budget and twin-world credit-assignment papers for cheaper, finer-grained learning signal; if you run on AWS, try the SageMaker Wordle pipeline before planning around it, and wait for Qwen's primary QwenGyre release.
